analysis.one_liner: Slaps federal refunds on nursing homes that provide substandard care and publishes their inspection and staffing records online.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2000 and referred to committee, where it stayed until Congress ended without ever reaching a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Nursing Home Quality Protection Act would have made nursing homes pay federal refunds—$2,000 to $25,000 per deficiency—when inspections find substandard care, with the money going into an account that funds state grants to hire and train more nurses. It would also require the government to post each home's inspection results, complaints, staffing levels, ownership, and labor violations on the internet, and would restore the Boren Amendment requirement that states pay nursing homes enough to deliver quality care. The bill never left committee before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families gain the most: stronger financial penalties for bad care, more staff paid for out of penalty refunds, and public access to each facility's inspection record, staffing ratios, complaints, ownership, and labor violations. Nursing home workers also gain, since the grant funds can be used to recruit, retain, and train nursing staff.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: It imposes automatic refunds on nursing homes for substandard care—$2,000 per deficiency that could cause harm, $10,000 for actual harm, and $25,000 for deficiencies putting a resident in immediate jeopardy—adjustable for inflation.
It channels all those refund and withheld-payment dollars into a Nursing Facility Quality Improvement Account, which funds state grants to recruit, retain, and train nursing staff.

It requires HHS to publish on the internet, updated at least every 90 days, each facility's inspection surveys, complaints, enforcement actions, staffing ratios, ownership and chain status, and labor violations.
It restores the Boren Amendment requirement that states pay nursing homes rates reasonable and adequate to provide quality care, undoing the 1997 repeal.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing homes that provide substandard care, through per-deficiency refunds and withheld federal payments; states and federal taxpayers, through the restored Boren Amendment requirement to pay nursing homes adequate Medicaid rates; and facilities facing new recordkeeping and reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing homes and, via Boren, state budgets

drawbacks.text: Restoring the Boren Amendment would obligate states to pay nursing homes 'reasonable and adequate' Medicaid rates, raising costs for state budgets and federal taxpayers without a precise measure of how much, and critics could argue higher payments do not automatically translate into better care.

The refund schedule ($2,000 to $25,000 per deficiency) applies to every surveyed deficiency, and facilities would bear new recordkeeping and reporting duties, which smaller operators could find burdensome even when the intent is to punish poor care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to nursing home residents—tougher financial penalties for bad care, more staff funded by those penalties, and public access to each home's inspection record—are substantial and the costs fall mainly on facilities that provide substandard care. The main drawback is the Boren restoration, which raises Medicaid spending for states and the federal government without any guarantee the money reaches direct care, and new federal requirements could strain small, rural facilities. On balance, the bill is well aimed at quality problems; its design flaw is the open-ended payment mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a vote: it sat in committee and its subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, and it died there.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2000, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce.
On August 8, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment—its last recorded action.
No further action, no markup, no floor vote is recorded before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died at the subcommittee stage.
The bill had 28 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to its Democratic sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing homes that provide substandard care avoided new federal penalties and public disclosure; no one else benefited.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors, plus the sponsor and the senior Democrats listed as original cosponsors, were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: The bill imposes per-deficiency refunds of $2,000 to $25,000, publicizes inspection records and staffing ratios, and can withhold federal payments from facilities that refuse to pay. Facilities providing quality care pay nothing.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators as a whole (via Medicaid rates)
industries.note: Restoring the Boren Amendment pushes states toward higher Medicaid payment rates, raising revenue for the industry broadly even as bad actors face penalties.
Quality Improvement grants may be used to recruit and retain nurses and aides and fund training, addressing chronic understaffing in the sector.
